content: Cache-aside loads data only after a miss: the application reads the cache, fetches from the database on a miss, then fills the cache. It is simple and avoids caching unread data, but first reads are slower and stale entries require an invalidation policy. Write-through updates cache and database together. Reads stay warm and consistency is easier to reason about, but every write pays extra latency and may cache data that is never read.

questions.prompt: Why might cache-aside be preferable for a read-heavy catalog with a long tail of rarely viewed products?
questions.reference_answer: It caches only requested products, conserves cache capacity, and keeps the application in control; limitations include cold misses and invalidation complexity.

questions.prompt: What failure mode appears if the database update succeeds but cache invalidation fails? How would you reduce the risk?
questions.reference_answer: Clients can read stale data. Use TTLs, retries, an outbox/event stream, versioned values, or delete-after-write policies depending on consistency requirements.

questions.prompt: When would write-through be a poor choice even though it improves read freshness?
questions.reference_answer: When writes are high-volume, write latency is sensitive, cache capacity is limited, or much written data is never read.

content: Modulo sharding maps a key with hash(key) % N, but changing N remaps most keys. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so membership changes move only a portion of keys. Virtual nodes give each physical node several ring positions, which improves balance and makes heterogeneous capacity easier to model. The trade-off is greater metadata and operational complexity.

questions.prompt: Why does modulo hashing behave badly when the cluster grows from N to N+1 nodes?
questions.reference_answer: The divisor changes, so most keys receive a new remainder and must move, causing cache misses or large-scale redistribution.

questions.prompt: What limitation of basic consistent hashing do virtual nodes address, and what new cost do they introduce?
questions.reference_answer: They reduce uneven key distribution and support capacity weighting, but add ring metadata and more ownership transitions to manage.

questions.prompt: When is simple modulo sharding still the better design?
questions.reference_answer: When membership is fixed, redistribution is already centrally managed, operational simplicity matters more, or the dataset is small enough to rebalance cheaply.
